## Title

A national-scale model for spatially explicit predictions of summertime methane emissions from reservoir water surfaces

## Authors

J.J. Beaulieu^1\*^, R.M. Pilla^2^, B.R. Deemer^3^, N.A. Griffiths^2^, J.W. Hollister^4^, A.O. Tatters^5^

^1^Office of Applied Sciences and Environmental Solutions, Environmental Protection Agency, Cincinnati, Ohio, USA\
^2^ Environmental Sciences Division, Oak Ridge National Laboratory, Oak Ridge, Tennessee, USA\
^3^ Southwest Biological Science Center, Grand Canyon Monitoring and Research Center, U.S. Geological Survey, Flagstaff, Arizona, USA\
^4^ Office of Applied Sciences and Environmental Solutions, Environmental Protection Agency, Narragansett, Rhode Island, USA\
^5^ University of Washington, Olympic Natural Resources Center, Forks, Washington, USA

\*corresponding author: beaulieu.jake\@epa.gov

## Abstract

Reservoirs are globally important sources of methane but the magnitude of their emissions is highly uncertain due, in part, to a lack of published measurements that were collected using consistent methodology across a broad range of reservoirs. Here we train random forest (RF) models using over 2,000 emission rate measurements from 146 U.S. reservoirs, which is the largest methodologically consistent dataset published to date. The RF models identified indices of reservoir morphometry as the most important predictors, with methane emission rates increasing with littoral zone extent and decreasing with reservoir surface area. Methane emission rates were also positively related to sediment organic carbon, but ebullition was suppressed at high sulfate concentrations. In contrast to earlier literature, we did not find strong relationships with indicators of phytoplankton abundance or reservoir age. Agreement between predicted and observed values was similar, or slightly better, than previously published models. However, it was substantially lower when the predictions, which were modeled at the log scale, were back-transformed to linear space. Predictive methane emission rate models are routinely trained using log scale data and our analysis highlights the importance of propagating prediction errors when back-transforming predictions for use in emission inventories. Prediction accuracy improved by approximately 10% when models were trained using *in-situ* measures of physicochemical parameters (e.g., depth, temperature) rather than values obtained from widely available datasets. Models presented here are suitable for making spatially-explicit predictions of emission rates within any U.S. reservoir, or for predicting reservoir-scale emission rates, depending on data availability.

## Introduction

Reservoirs are globally important sources of CH~4~ to the atmosphere. Recent estimates suggest that they contribute \~3.5% of global CH~4~ emissions and make up \~50% of anthropogenic freshwater sources, yet their contribution is not well constrained [@canadell_etal_2021; @rosentreter_etal_2021; @saunois_etal_2025]. Global estimates of CH~4~ emissions from reservoir water surfaces vary more than threefold, from 4.8 to 18.7 Tg CH~4~ yr^-1^ [@lauerwald_etal_2023], with an additional 6.7 to 37.1 Tg CH~4~ yr^-1^ from degassing at dam turbines [@harrison_etal_2021].

Several statistical and process-based models of reservoir CH~4~ emission rates are available for estimating emissions at regional, national, and global scales [@prairie_2021; @johnson_etal_2021; @beaulieu_et_al_2020; @zhuang_2023; @tan_2024; @maisonnier_2025; @delwiche_etal_2022]. These models are largely based on published measurements of areal CH~4~ emission rates (e.g. mg CH~4~ m^-2^ d^-1^) and therefore suffer from the same sources of uncertainty that pertain to the original measurements, including deficiencies in the CH~4~ emission pathways that were measured and/or the spatio-temporal resolution of the measurements. Methane can be emitted to the atmosphere via multiple pathways including diffusion, ebullition (bubbling), degassing, and translocation through emergent vegetation. Diffusion and ebullition often dominate reservoir-scale emissions, although degassing emissions can approach the magnitude of diffusion and ebullition in deep, productive reservoirs subject to hypolimnetic withdrawal [@jager_etal_2022; @johnson_etal_2021; @harrison_etal_2021]. However, these CH~4~ emission pathways are rarely measured simultaneously [@jager_etal_2022] and measurement methodologies vary among studies, complicating comprehensive upscaling efforts [@saunois_etal_2025]. Many early studies of reservoir CH~4~ only measured diffusive emissions (see discussion in Deemer et al. [-@deemer_et_al_2016]), but studies that have quantified both diffusion and ebullition reveal that ebullition is often dominant (median of 78% of total flux; @deemer_2021) albeit highly variable (0 to nearly 100%).

Failure to capture spatio-temporal variability in CH~4~ emission rates within and across systems can limit the accuracy of emission models. Methane ebullition is a spatio-temporally variable emission pathway [@linkhorst_etal_2020] that often requires sampling at high temporal and spatial resolutions [@wik_2016] and can be difficult to distinguish from diffusive emissions via common sampling techniques like floating chambers [@minaudo_2026]. Studies often find that ebullition is higher at shallow depths (\~ \<10 m) due to lower hydrostatic pressure, allowing bubbles to rise to the water surface more readily [@west_2016]. The shorter transport distance through the water column also limits bubble dissolution and the opportunity for oxidation [@mcginnis_2006]. However, even within shallower areas, ebullition is highly sporadic, and regions with higher rates of sedimentation [@maeck_2013] and/or primary productivity [@linkhorst_2021], such as tributary inflows [@delsontro_2011; @beaulieu_etal_2016; @de_mello_2018], often experience higher ebullitive emission rates. Diffusive emission rates can also exhibit strong spatial patterning within individual reservoirs [@beaulieu_etal_2016; @hoffman_2013]. While many studies have documented these spatial patterns, most models for predicting reservoir emissions are trained on measurements that were aggregated to the reservoir scale, regardless of the spatial resolution or site selection criteria employed in the original studies. This approach possibly biases the data and adds uncertainty to model predictions. Furthermore, models trained using reservoir-scale data are not well suited for predicting the spatial distribution of CH~4~ emission rates within a given reservoir, limiting their utility for investigating CH~4~ emission rates in specific reservoirs.

Another limitation of existing models is that they are developed based on data collected via different methodologies and from small populations of lakes and reservoirs. Existing studies may also be biased towards particular types of reservoirs (e.g., hydropower, boreal), failing to adequately represent the full population [@deemer_2021]. Hence, comprehensive studies that apply uniform methodology across many probabilistically selected reservoirs with varying characteristics are needed to better constrain CH~4~ emission rate estimates and improve model predictions.

In this study, we carried out a comprehensive assessment of diffusive and ebullitive CH~4~ emission rates from 146 reservoirs across the conterminous U.S. (CONUS) and Puerto Rico, comprising over 2000 measurements of each emission pathway. Although there is growing evidence that degassing can be an important emission pathway, it was not measured in this assessment due to logisitical constraints. The sampled reservoirs were selected using a probabilistic survey design stratified by ecoregion, reservoir size and trophic status [@beaulieu_et_al_2026]. We utilized uniform methodology to measure CH~4~ diffusion and ebullition at multiple probabilistically selected locations in each reservoir during the summer and also collected physicochemical measurements used to build predictive relationships. Our aims were to 1) use the new dataset to train spatially explicit models for predicting emission rates within and across CONUS reservoirs, and 2) quantify the loss in predictive power when local-scale waterbody measurements (e.g., site-specific water chemistry, chlorophyll-*a* concentrations, etc.) are unavailable and large-scale datasets (e.g., Globathy [@khazaei_2022], lake Cat [@hill_et_al_2018]) are used instead. In addition to model development and model comparison, we examine the relative contribution of ebullition vs. diffusion and describe unique patterns in national-scale CH~4~ emissions that emerged from this survey.

## Methods

### Data sources

We used data from the Survey of Reservoir Greenhouse gas Emissions (SuRGE) project containing CH~4~ emission rates measured at `r dat_trans %>% group_by(lake_id) %>% summarize(n_site = n()) %>% {min(.$n_site)}` to `r dat_trans %>% group_by(lake_id) %>% summarize(n_site = n()) %>% {max(.$n_site)}` locations within each of 146 U.S. reservoirs [@beaulieu_et_al_2026]. One hundred and eight of these reservoirs were selected using a generalized random-tessellation (GRTS) design [@stevens_et_al_2004], were included in the U.S. EPA's 2017 National Lakes Assessment [@usepa_2022], and represent a spatially balanced, representative sample of reservoirs across the CONUS. Thirty two of the reservoirs in Ohio, Kentucky, and Indiana were sampled in an earlier effort to characterize emission rates across a land use and maximum depth gradient [@beaulieu_et_al_2020]. The remaining `r 146-108-32 %>% as.english(.)` reservoirs were selected based on special interest (e.g., reference sites, location of related research). Sampling sites within each reservoir were selected using a within-reservoir GRTS design that, in some cases, was stratified to ensure the placement of sampling sites in areas where high emission rates were expected (e.g., river inflows). All reservoirs were sampled once during the summers of 2016-2023, with `r dat_trans %>% filter(visit == 2) %>% distinct(lake_id) %>% {nrow(.)} %>% as.english(.)` reservoirs visited twice (lake_id = `r dat_trans %>% filter(visit == 2) %>% distinct(lake_id) %>% pull %>% as.character() %>% as.numeric(.) %>% paste(., collapse = ", ")` in dataset).

Diffusive CH~4~ emission rates were measured using short-term (`r min(dat_trans$ch4_deployment_length, na.rm = TRUE)` - `r max(dat_trans$ch4_deployment_length, na.rm = TRUE)` seconds: mean = `r mean(dat_trans$ch4_deployment_length, na.rm = TRUE) %>% round(., 0)` seconds) floating chamber deployments. Ebullitive CH~4~ emissions were measured using inverted funnels deployed for `r dat_trans %>% mutate(duration = trap_rtrvl_date_time - trap_deply_date_time) %>% {min(.$duration, na.rm = TRUE)} %>% as.numeric(.) %>% round(., digits = 1)` - `r dat_trans %>% mutate(duration = trap_rtrvl_date_time - trap_deply_date_time) %>% {max(.$duration, na.rm = TRUE)} %>% as.numeric(.) %>% round(., digits = 1)` hours (mean = `r dat_trans %>% mutate(duration = trap_rtrvl_date_time - trap_deply_date_time) %>% {mean(.$duration, na.rm = TRUE)} %>% as.numeric(.) %>% round(., digits = 1)` hours). Vertically resolved temperature and dissolved oxygen profiles, nutrient concentrations (nitrogen, phosphorus, organic carbon, sulfate), and chlorophyll-*a* (extraction-based) were measured at the deepest sampling site in each reservoir. Basic physicochemistry parameters (temperature, dissolved oxygen, pH, optical sensor-based chlorophyll-*a*) and water depth were measured at all sites. See Beaulieu et al. [-@beaulieu_et_al_2026] for full methodological details.

In addition to variables measured during the sampling campaign, the SuRGE dataset contains numerous predictor variables derived from external sources. Reservoir age was derived from the National Inventory of Dams [@usace_2025] supplemented with historical sources, sediment carbon (C) content and water residence time were retrieved from the 2017 National Lakes Assessment [@usepa_2022], landscape and mean annual climate variables (e.g., watershed size, soil organic matter content, mean annual precipitation) were retrieved from lakeCat [@hill_et_al_2018], meteorology variables corresponding to the time and location of the emission rate observations were retrieved from ERA5-Land [@era5_2021], and remotely sensed trophic status and dissolved organic carbon (DOC) estimates were retrieved from LAGOS [@hanly_et_al_2025]. Given the potential for light to influence emissions via the inhibition of methanotrophy [@thottathil_2018], we supplemented the SuRGE dataset with shortwave radiation data accessed using the Free Weather API (https://open-meteo.com), a wrapper for ERA5-Land. Shortwave radiation was calculated as the sum of radiation during the duration of our observations in units of mJ m^-2^.

While sulfate (SO~4~^2-^) and chlorophyll-*a* samples were collected for most SuRGE reservoirs included in the probabilistic survey, SO~4~^2-^ was not collected in 2016 or early 2020 sampling campaigns, and chlorophyll-*a* was not measured at a subset of the 2016 survey sites. Because preliminary analysis suggested that both of these variables may be important predictors, we added auxiliary data for missing SO~4~^2-^ (n = `r dat_raw %>% filter(is.na(so4_shallow)) %>% distinct(lake_id) %>% {nrow(.)}`) and extraction-based chlorophyll-*a* (n = `r dat_raw %>% filter(is.na(chla_lab_shallow)) %>% distinct(lake_id) %>% {nrow(.)}`) concentrations with values obtained from state (e.g., Ohio Department of Natural Resources) or federal (U.S. Army Corps of Engineers, EPA's National Lakes Assessment) monitoring programs. Preference was given to values measured during the same month and year of the emission rate measurements when available, otherwise the mean of all available data was used. Potential error from assigning missing observations with values from external data sources was assessed by comparing values measured during the SuRGE campaign to those measured during the 2017 and 2022 National Lakes Assessments [@usepa_2022; @usepa_2024] in reservoirs where both values were available. The Pearson correlation coefficient (*r*) among chlorophyll-*a* measurements was `r dat_raw %>% select(chla_lab_shallow, nla17_chla, nla22_chla) %>% distinct %>% pivot_longer(!chla_lab_shallow) %>% {cor(.$chla_lab_shallow, .$value, use = "complete.obs") %>% round(digits = 2)}`. Sulfate showed much less temporal variability with an *r* value of `r dat_raw %>% select(so4_shallow, nla17_sulfate, nla22_sulfate) %>% distinct %>% pivot_longer(!so4_shallow) %>% {cor(.$so4_shallow, .$value, use = "complete.obs") %>% round(digits = 2)}`.

### Predictor variables and modeling approach

Predictor variables representing reservoir morphometry, tropic status, climate, hydrology, watershed, and chemical patterns were selected for use in modeling (**Table 1**). Variables within each group were assessed for collinearity using variance inflation factor (VIF) values [@montgomery_peck_1992]. Variables with the greatest VIF were removed until all variables had a VIF < 3. The collection of variables used in each model were screened for collinearity using the same approach. Several morphological variables were collinear and we chose *a priori* to include surface area as a predictor while omitting all other morphological variables with a VIF \> 3 (see Supplemental Methods for more detail). We also excluded some variables that were originally compiled [@beaulieu_et_al_2026], but had high missingness.

Model predictor sets were constructed for each response variable (diffusive, ebullitive, and total CH~4~ emission rates: mg CH~4~ m^-2^ d^-1^) using two approaches (**Table 1**). The first “national” model set used predictors that are available in national databases for many U.S. reservoirs. The second “local” set of models supplemented, or replaced, the national predictors with those directly measured during the SuRGE or prior sampling campaigns (e.g., National Lakes Assessment). For example, the national model included remotely sensed estimates of chlorophyll-*a*, which are widely available for the U.S. [@hanly_et_al_2025], whereas the local model used direct *in-situ* measurements of chlorophyll-*a*. For the local model, estimates of reservoir morphology (surface area, maximum depth, mean depth, and littoral fraction) were informed by *in-situ* measurements of site depth and field-verified estimates of surface area [@beaulieu_et_al_2026]. For the national model, we estimated maximum depth, mean depth, and littoral fraction using GLOBathy (n=126; @khazaei_2022), the National Hydrography Dataset (n=13), LAGOS (n=5; @cheruvelil_2021), the National Lakes Assessment 2017 (n=1) and the National Lakes Assessment 2012 (n=1). Littoral fraction was defined as the proportion of the reservoir \< 2.5 m deep [@usfws_2023]. We estimated surface area for the national model using the National Hydrography Dataset (n=143; @McKay_2012) and Hydrolakes (n=3; @messager_2016).

Comparing these two sets of models determined how much prediction accuracy improves when investigators expend resources to conduct an "on the ground" investigation, rather than relying exclusively on widely available data. Emission rate observations with missing values for any predictors were removed prior to modeling, and the final number of observations per model ranged from `r min(table2_object$table2_dat$nobs)` - `r max(table2_object$table2_dat$nobs)` (**Table 2**). No missing values were imputed during the modeling.

Random forest (RF) models [@breiman_2001], a machine learning technique, were used to relate CH~4~ emission rates (diffusive, ebullitive, total) to predictor variables **(Table 1)**. This method was chosen because it can accommodate non-linear relationships and interactions, both of which are present in the data. Random forests are a collection of regression trees, where each tree is trained on a bootstrapped sample of the data and predictor variables. Predictions from the RF model are an average of the predictions across the individual trees. Model error for each tree in the RF is quantified by comparing the observations that were withheld from each tree by the bootstrap sampling procedure, to the value predicted for those observations. These prediction errors are averaged across the ensemble of trees and reported as the out-of-bag (OOB) model error.

In total, we ran six RF models, one for each emission mechanism (diffusion, ebullition, and total) and predictor variable set (national and local). Response variables were log transformed to optimize model fitting and prediction because non-constant variation across regression tree residuals gives greater weight to higher variance data [@death_fabricius_2000]. When reported on the linear scale, model predictions and standard errors were back-transformed using the Miller [@miller_1984] and delta [@oehlert_1992] methods, respectively, to minimize bias in log to linear transformations. RF modeling was conducted using the ranger package [@wright_ziegler_2017] in R version 4.5.0 [@r_core_team_2025] with four predictor variables randomly sampled at each split (mtry argument), a minimum of five observations per node (min.node.size argument), and a total of 500 trees per RF (num.trees argument).

The relative importance of predictor variables was ranked using the permutation variable importance method [@breiman_2001; @wright_et_al_2016]. Permutation variable importance was calculated using a two-step method. In the first step, the OOB performance was calculated for each tree. In the second step, the values for the predictor variable of interest were randomly permuted, and the OOB performance recalculated. The difference between the two OOB values was the permuted importance for the variable of interest. This procedure was repeated for each variable and the permuted importance values averaged across all trees. Relationships between response and predictor values were further investigated using partial dependence plots (PDPs) which show the marginal effect of a single predictor on the response while accounting for the average effect of the other predictors in the model [@friedman_2001].

We used multiple metrics to quantify model explanatory power, prediction error, and bias. Model explanatory power was quantified as the coefficient of determination (r^2^) between observed and predicted. Absolute magnitude of the prediction error was quantified as root mean square error (RMSE) and mean absolute error (MAE). Mean absolute error is less influenced by outliers than RMSE. We report the symmetric mean absolute percentage error (sMAPE) as a metric of relative error between predicted and observed. sMAPE is more robust than mean absolute percentage error (MAPE) when values approach zero (we observed many zero values for CH~4~ ebullition) [@armstrong_1985]. Model bias was quantified as mean fractional bias (MFB):

$$
MFB = \frac{2}{N} \sum_{i=1}^{N} \frac{\text{predicted}_i - \text{observed}_i}{\text{predicted}_i + \text{observed}_i} * 100
$$

where N is the number of observations in the model. MFB ranges between -200% and 200%, with negative and positive values indicating model under and overprediction, respectively [@boylan_russell]. Model performance metrics were calculated separately for 1) observations and predictions on the log scale, and 2) linear scale observations and model predictions back-transformed to linear space using the Miller correction. All metrics of model performance were calculated using OOB predictions.

We used the local RF model to make spatially explicit predictions of total CH~4~ emission rates in William H. Harsha Lake, a reservoir in southwest Ohio (lake_id 1031 in SuRGE dataset). Model predictions were driven by a combination of spatially invariant and spatially variable predictors. Reservoir-scale predictors, including surface area and littoral fraction, were constant across the reservoir. Site-specific predictors (e.g., chlorophyll-*a*, turbidity, temperature, dissolved oxygen, depth) were mapped across the reservoir when the data were available. Bathymetry was retrieved from the Ohio Department of Natural Resources Geospatial Data Portal and point measurements of chlorophyll-*a*, turbidity, and surface water temperature in June 2014 were retrieved from Beck et al. [-@beck_2016]. Point measurements of dissolved oxygen and water temperature between June and August of 2015 were retrieved from Beaulieu et al. [-@beaulieu_etal_2018]. Point observations of sediment C content were retrieved from Berberich et al. [-@berberich_2019]. Point observations of predictor variables were extrapolated across the reservoir surface by 1) fitting a spatial linear model (splm) to each variable using site depth as the predictor, and 2) using the model to predict the value of each variable across a spatial grid bounded by the lake perimeter. The splm and spatial predictions were executed using the spmodel package [@dumelle_et_al_2023] in R version 4.5.0. The spatially invariant and spatially variable predictors were fed into the local RF model for total CH~4~ to generate spatially explicit emission rate and standard error predictions across the reservoir extent. The spmodel package includes an implementation of RF regression Kriging [@fox_etal_2020] where 1) spatially explicit residuals from a RF are modeled with a semivariaogram and extrapolated across unsampled areas using Kriging, and 2) the predicted residuals are added to spatially explicit RF predictions. This approach can improve prediction accuracy when there is spatial structure in the RF residuals. Semivariograms of RF residuals showed no evidence of spatial structure in the models presented here and the William H. Harsha Lake total CH~4~ emission rate predictions were made using the RF as implemented in the ranger package.

## Results

### Emission Rates and Spatial Patterns

Total CH~4~ emission rates ranged from `r emissions_lake_data %>% slice_min(ch4_total_lake) %>% pull(ch4_total_lake) %>% round(., 1)` - `r emissions_lake_data %>% slice_max(ch4_total_lake) %>% pull(ch4_total_lake) %>% round(., 1)` mg CH~4~ m^-2^ d^-1^ and diffusion was greater than ebullition at `r dat_trans %>% mutate(diff_greater = ch4_diffusion > ch4_ebullition) %>% group_by(diff_greater) %>% summarize(counts = NROW(diff_greater)) %>% filter(!is.na(diff_greater)) %>% pivot_wider(values_from = counts, names_from = diff_greater) %>% rename("less" = 1, "great" = 2) %>% mutate(percent = great / (great + less)*100) %>% pull(percent) %>% {round(., 1)}`% of sites. Spatial patterning in total CH~4~ emission rates, and in the proportion of diffusion versus ebullition, was evident across the U.S. **(Figure 1)**. Notably, the lake-wide proportion of total CH~4~ emissions as ebullition (compared to diffusion) generally increased from west to east (Pearson's r between percent ebullition and longitude = `r cor(lake_scale_percent_ebul$long, lake_scale_percent_ebul$percent_ebul, use = "pairwise.complete.obs") %>% round(2)`), with low relative ebullition contributions in the western U.S. that increased in the central U.S. and Midwest to the Atlantic coast **(Figure S1A)**. Two key drivers that would typically promote ebullition in lieu of diffusion (SO~4~^2-^ and mean depth) both showed general decreases from west to east (r = `r cor(lake_scale_percent_ebul$long, lake_scale_percent_ebul$so4_shallow, use = "pairwise.complete.obs") %>% round(2)`, r = `r cor(lake_scale_percent_ebul$long, lake_scale_percent_ebul$mean_depth, use = "pairwise.complete.obs") %>% round(2)`, respectively). Still, only SO~4~^2-^ was clearly related to the ebullition percent contribution in this analysis (r = `r cor(lake_scale_percent_ebul$so4_shallow, lake_scale_percent_ebul$percent_ebul, use = "pairwise.complete.obs") %>% round(2)`; **Figure S1B**). Sulfate was higher in the western U.S. and associated with much lower ebullition percent contribution (i.e., greater diffusive contribution), whereas reservoirs with lower SO~4~^2-^ (\< \~100 mg L^-1^), more common in the central to eastern U.S., had a wide range of ebullition percent contribution, including most of the lakes with 75-100% of total CH~4~ emissions from ebullition.

### Random Forest Models

The OOB r^2^ of the local RF models, when evaluated on the log response scale, ranged from `r table2_object$table2_dat %>% filter(model_var_set == "local_vars_all") %>% {round(min(.$r2_log), 2)}` to `r table2_object$table2_dat %>% filter(model_var_set == "local_vars_all") %>% {round(max(.$r2_log), 2)}` and were, on average, `r table2_object$table2_dat %>% select(response, model_var_set, r2_log) %>%  pivot_wider(names_from = model_var_set, values_from = r2_log) %>% mutate(diff = local_vars_all - global_vars) %>% summarize(mean_diff = mean(diff)) %>% pull %>% round(., 2)` greater than the corresponding national model **(Table 2)**. When the OOB predictions were back-transformed to the linear scale and compared to the observations, the OOB r^2^ values were considerably lower for both local (mean r^2^ = `r table2_object$table2_dat %>% filter(model_var_set == "local_vars_all") %>% {round(mean(.$r2_linear), 2)}`) and national (mean r^2^ = `r table2_object$table2_dat %>% filter(model_var_set == "global_vars") %>% {round(mean(.$r2_linear), 2)}`) models **(Figure S2)**. Log-scale measures of absolute error (RMSE, MAE) were greater for the national than local models, but no consistent pattern was evident when these metrics were calculated on the linear scale of the response. The symmetric mean absolute percentage error (sMAPE) was greater when calculated on the linear-scale of the response, relative to the log scale, was greater for ebullition than diffusion and total, and was 5-10% greater in the national versus local models. Model predictions of diffusive and total emission rates were essentially unbiased on the log scale (MFB \< `r table2_object$table2_dat %>% filter(grepl(c("diffusion|total"), response)) %>% {mean(.$fbias_log)} %>% ceiling(.)`%) but positively biased when back-transformed to the linear scale (MFB range: `r table2_object$table2_dat %>% filter(grepl(c("diffusion|total"), response)) %>% {min(.$fbias_linear)} %>% round(., 1)` - `r table2_object$table2_dat %>% filter(grepl(c("diffusion|total"), response)) %>% {max(.$fbias_linear)} %>% round(., 1)`%) **(Table 2, Figure S2)**. Ebullition rate predictions were biased high in log (mean MFB `r table2_object$table2_dat %>% filter(grepl("ebullition", response)) %>% {mean(.$fbias_log)} %>% round(., 1)`%) and linear space (mean MFB `r table2_object$table2_dat %>% filter(grepl("ebullition", response)) %>% {mean(.$fbias_linear)} %>% round(., 1)`%).

The most important variable identified in the local RF models for all three emission mechanisms was littoral fraction **(Figure 2)**. Mean depth was the second most important variable for total and ebullition, and third most important for diffusion. For total and diffusive CH~4~ emission rates, sediment C was the third and second most important variable identified, respectively. For ebullition, site depth was the third most important predictor variable identified. Following these three clearly most important variables (relative importance \> 0.65), total and diffusion had total nitrogen (TN), surface area, and buoyancy frequency identified as the next set of moderately important variables, while CH~4~ ebullition had SO~4~^2-^, and deep temperature. Notably, reservoir age was overall a weak predictor for all three emission mechanisms (relative importance 0.31-0.45) **(Figure S3)**.

Consistent with local models, the national models identified littoral fraction, depth, carbon (dissolved organic carbon (DOC)), and surface area as important predictors **(Figure S4)**. National models also identified a few important predictors not highlighted in the local models. For example, the national model for total CH~4~ emission rates also identified maximum air temperature, DOC (remotely sensed), and relative drainage area as top predictors. The national diffusive emission rate model identified maximum air temperature as an important predictor. The national ebullition rate model identified elevation as the most important predictor, followed distantly by precipitation and chlorophyll-*a* (remotely sensed).

The three emission pathways showed similar patterns in response to the most important variables identified in the local RF models, albeit of different mean magnitudes, as indicated by partial dependence plots **(Figure 3)**. Rates of all emission pathways showed non-linear responses to increasing littoral fraction, where emission rates were fairly static up to \~75% littoral fraction, above which emission rates were predicted to significantly increase. Methane emission rates were predicted to decrease with increasing mean reservoir depth, with steepest declines between 0-5 m, and less change at depths \>10-15 m. Methane emission rates increased with sediment C (note this was not a top predictor for ebullition) up to approximately % sediment C content beyond which emission rates were relatively stable. Sulfate was a moderate predictor of ebullition (**Figure 2**) with rates declining steeply between 0 and \~300 mg SO~4~^2-^ L^-1^; but the other two emission mechanisms did not show a strong decline with increasing SO~4~^2-^ . Finally, surface area was a moderate predictor of diffusive, ebullitive, and total CH~4~ emission rates, wherein emission rates were predicted to be greatest in smaller waterbodies and to decrease relatively linearly as waterbody size increased.

### Interactions

We found an interaction between mean depth and sediment C in the local total emission rate model **(Figure 4)**. Total emission rates were greatest in shallow lakes with C-rich sediment and lowest in deep lakes with C-poor sediment. The greatest change in the total emission rate occurred across the low range in sediment C (0-5%) and low range in mean depth (0-5 m), above which predicted total emission rates were generally stable.

When sediment C was at its lowest (blue line at bottom right of **Figure 4**), total emission rates ranged from `r interaction_results[[1]] %>% filter(group == 1) %>% summarize(min = expm1(min(yhat))) %>% round(., 1)` to `r interaction_results[[1]] %>% filter(group == 1) %>% summarize(max = expm1(max(yhat))) %>% round(., 1)` mg CH~4~ m^-2^ d^-1^ as mean depth varied. When sediment C was at its highest (blue line at upper left of **Figure 4**), the total emission rate ranged from `r interaction_results[[1]] %>% filter(group == 50) %>% summarize(min = expm1(min(yhat))) %>% round(., 1)` to `r interaction_results[[1]] %>% filter(group == 50) %>% summarize(max = expm1(max(yhat))) %>% round(., 1)` mg CH~4~ m^-2^ d^-1^ as mean depth varied. This corresponds to a 56% higher range in total emission rate along a gradient of mean depths when sediment C was high compared to when low. Conversely, when mean depth was at its lowest (red line at upper right in **Figure 4**), total emission rates ranged from `r interaction_results[[2]] %>% filter(group == 1) %>% summarize(min = expm1(min(yhat))) %>% round(., 1)` to `r interaction_results[[2]] %>% filter(group == 1) %>% summarize(max = expm1(max(yhat))) %>% round(., 1)` mg CH~4~ m^-2^ d^-1^ as sediment C varied. When mean depth was at its greatest (red line at bottom left in **Figure 4**), total emission rate ranged from `r interaction_results[[2]] %>% filter(group == 50) %>% summarize(min = expm1(min(yhat))) %>% round(., 1)` to `r interaction_results[[2]] %>% filter(group == 50) %>% summarize(max = expm1(max(yhat))) %>% round(., 1)` mg CH~4~ m^-2^ d^-1^ as sediment C varied. This corresponded to a 43% higher range in total emission rate along a gradient of sediment C when mean depth was shallower compared to when deeper.

### Spatially Explicit Application of the Local Random Forest Model

The RF model predicted total CH~4~ emission rates in William H. Harsha Lake ranging from 70.9 - 109.2 mg CH~4~ m^-2^ d^-1^ **(Figure 5A)**. The standard error of the predictions ranged from 9.6 - 18.3 mg CH~4~ m^-2^ d^-1^ **(Figure 5B)**. Strong spatial patterning in the predictions was evident with high emission rates predicted in the shallow eastern basin and low emission rates in the deep western basin.

## Discussion

Total CH~4~ emission rates varied by `r (dat_trans %>% slice_max(ch4_total) %>% pull(ch4_total) / dat_trans %>% slice_min(ch4_total) %>% pull(ch4_total)) %>% log10(.) %>% ceiling(.) %>% xfun::numbers_to_words(.)` orders of magnitude across the CONUS and Puerto Rico, showing strong longitudinal gradients in relative contributions of ebullition versus diffusion, and this variability could be well explained with our RF models with \<20% error (on the log scale; **Table 2**). Reservoir-scale measures of morphometry were the most important predictors for all three CH~4~ emission pathways and sediment C was one of the top three predictors for diffusion and total emission rates. Biogeochemical variables such as chlorophyll-*a* and SO~4~^2-^ that have previously been linked with CH~4~ emission rates in reservoirs, wetlands, and lakes [@deemer_et_al_2016; @delsontro_2018; @bansal_2023; @soued_2024] were not among the most important predictors of emission rates in this national-scale study, although SO~4~^2-^ was a moderately important predictor of ebullition (described below). Further, collecting *in-situ* data improved explanatory power and predictive capabilities by \~10%, on average, as compared to models that were restricted to predictors in readily available datasets. This, together with the interaction we report between sediment C and mean depth, suggests *in-situ* data collection efforts focused on shallow reservoirs with high littoral fraction and high sediment C may be most useful in constraining CH~4~ estimates from likely high-emitting waterbodies. While the local model developed here contained only one lakewide value for percent sediment C, some reservoirs may exhibit large spatial gradients in sediment C; spatially resolved measurements of sediment C together with CH~4~ emission rate measurements may further constrain the relationship.

### Model Predictors

#### Morphometry

Measures of reservoir morphometry were important predictors of CH~4~ emission rates across all models, which is consistent with previous work at global [@delsontro_beaulieu_2018; @deemer_2021], regional [@west_2016], and site-specific scales [@desrosiers_2022]. The local models identified mean reservoir depth as the second or third most important predictor **(Figure 2)**, with all emission pathways (diffusion, ebullition, total) exhibiting a steep, non-linear decline in emission rates with increasing mean depth **(Figure 3)**. Diffusive emission rates fell sharply as mean reservoir depth increased from a minimum of `r dat_trans %>% {min(.$mean_depth, na.rm = TRUE)}` m, the shallowest waterbody in the dataset, to about 2.5 m, with very low emission rates beyond depths of about 12 m. These depth thresholds roughly align with a recent global study that estimated 85% of diffusive CH~4~ fluxes originate from lakes with a mean depth \<5 m [@li_2020]. This pattern may reflect the relatively greater abundance of vegetated littoral zones, a known hot spot for CH~4~ production, in shallower reservoirs [@delsontro_2018; @desrosiers_2022]. This explanation is supported by the RF models which identified the fraction of the waterbody \<2.5 m deep, the functional definition of the littoral zone used in this study, as the single most important predictor of CH~4~ emission rates for all pathways. While mean reservoir depth was an important predictor of diffusive emission rates, site-specific depth measurements were overall much less important. This may be because dissolved CH~4~, which drives diffusive emissions, can be widely advected throughout a waterbody. For example, CH~4~ produced in littoral sediment can be advected to the center of deep waterbodies before diffusing across the air-water interface [@delsontro_2018], thereby decoupling the depth of CH~4~ production from the depth of CH~4~ emission. By contrast, ebullitive emissions occur at the site of CH~4~ production and the RF identified site-depth as the third most important predictor for this emission pathway, with very minimal bubbling at depths deeper than \~10m. This is likely because CH~4~ contained in bubbles will dissolve into the water column as bubbles rise from the sediment and only a fraction of the original bubble CH~4~ will reach the atmosphere [@mcginnis_2006]. Bubble dissolution increases with water depth which likely contributes to the pattern of decreasing ebullition with increasing depth.

Total CH~4~ emission rates reflect the sum of diffusive and ebullitive emission rates, thus the factors controlling total emission rates are a blend of those controlling diffusion and ebullition. Site depth was not identified as an important predictor of total CH~4~ emission rates, likely because, on average, diffusion contributed more to total emissions than ebullition (diffusion was greater than ebullition at `r dat_trans %>% mutate(diff_greater = ch4_diffusion > ch4_ebullition) %>% group_by(diff_greater) %>% summarize(counts = NROW(diff_greater)) %>% filter(!is.na(diff_greater)) %>% pivot_wider(values_from = counts, names_from = diff_greater) %>% rename("less" = 1, "great" = 2) %>% mutate(percent = great / (great + less)*100) %>% pull(percent) %>% {round(., 1)}`% of sites). The RF model predicts a steep decline in total emission rates as mean depth increases to approximately 5 m. Five m was recently proposed as a threshold above or below which lakes, ponds, and wetlands show non-linear changes in a variety of ecosystem metrics, although no such threshold was found specifically for CH~4~ [@richardson_2022].

The importance of mean reservoir depth was also apparent in the models restricted to predictor variables that are widely available across the U.S. (“national" models; **Figure S4**). Estimates of mean depth are available for many U.S. waterbodies in the NHDPlusV2 database and across the globe in the GLOBathy dataset [@khazaei_2022]. At the global scale, previous work has found maximum depth to be a more informative predictor of total emissions than mean depth, but this was based on a very small sample size (n=9 reservoirs, [@deemer_2021]). Due to strong collinearity among morphological variables, maximum depth was excluded from our national models.

All emission pathways exhibited a non-linear, negative relationship with reservoir surface area, the fourth to fifth most important predictor in total and diffusive local and national models (10th and 14th for ebullitive local and national models, respectively). This result reinforces reports from numerous studies showing negative correlations between surface area and measures of CH~4~ biogeochemistry including emission rates and dissolved concentrations [@casas_ruiz_2021; @deemer_2021; @beaulieu_et_al_2020; @rasilo_et_al_2015].

Attributing a mechanism to the correlation between surface area and CH~4~ emission rates is difficult because of strong collinearity among indices of reservoir size and shape. We decided *a priori* to include surface area as a predictor to the exclusion of other morphology indices with a VIF \> 3. However, replacement of surface area with excluded variables, including shoreline complexity and dynamic ratio, results in models with nearly identical predictive accuracy (**Table S1**), but slightly different mechanistic interpretations. Surface area therefore serves as a proxy for several morphological indices and the correlation with CH~4~ emission rates is likely driven by a combination of mechanisms including a tendency for smaller reservoirs to be shallower, more likely to develop an anoxic hypolimnion due to higher sediment-to-volume ratios, and to have stronger connections between littoral and pelagic zones. The novel contribution of our finding is that it is supported by observations from the largest, most diverse, and most geographically distributed set of reservoirs analyzed to date, demonstrating that reservoir morphology plays a critical role in regulating CH~4~ biogeochemistry at broad geographic scales.

#### Carbon

The relationship between total and diffusive CH~4~ emission rates and sediment C likely results from sediment serving as a C source for methanogenesis [@bastviken_2008; @bodmer_2025]. A study across 72 aquatic systems found that sediment CH~4~ production potential was strongly related to the percent organic C in the sediments, while also noting a \> 4-fold higher potential CH~4~ production rate in reservoir sediments than lakes [@bodmer_2025]. While sediment C concentrations may be highly variable within a reservoir [@berberich_2019], the National Lakes Assessment (NLA) measurements used here were collected at the deepest point near the middle of the reservoir. Thus, the NLA sediment C represents a spatially invariant but consistent metric of sediment C availability. The response of CH~4~ emission rates to increasing sediment C availability is constrained by depth, however, with shallow reservoirs responding more strongly than deep systems. The interaction plot **(Figure 4)** reveals that when mean depth is at its lowest, total CH~4~ emission rates increased by `r interaction_results[[1]] %>% filter(group %in% c(1, 50)) %>% group_by(group, var1_name) %>% summarize(range_ch4 = expm1(max(yhat)) - expm1(min(yhat))) %>% pivot_wider(values_from = range_ch4, names_from = group) %>% pull(3) %>% {round(., 1)}` mg CH~4~ m^-2^ h^-1^ as sediment C increased, compared to an increase of only `r interaction_results[[1]] %>% filter(group %in% c(1, 50)) %>% group_by(group, var1_name) %>% summarize(range_ch4 = expm1(max(yhat)) - expm1(min(yhat))) %>% pivot_wider(values_from = range_ch4, names_from = group) %>% pull(2) %>% {round(., 1)}` mg CH~4~ m^-2^ h^-1^ when sediment C increased in the deepest waterbodies. This near-doubling of the CH~4~ emission rate response in shallow lakes with increasing sediment C highlights the magnitude of this interaction. This interaction likely occurs because sediment C drives rates of CH~4~ production while depth partially controls the fate of the produced CH~4~. Only a fraction of sediment-produced CH~4~ is emitted to the atmosphere, with the balance being oxidized or stored in the sediment. Storage is more important in deeper reservoirs due to the greater hydrostatic pressure at the sediment-water interface. Increasing water depth indirectly promotes CH~4~ oxidation by 1) increasing the fraction of bubble CH~4~ that dissolves in the water, and 2) increasing the water residence time of dissolved CH~4~ thereby allowing for a greater fraction of the dissolved CH~4~ to be oxidized. However, water residence time (estimated based on \$\\delta\$^18^O; @brooks_2024) was not a top predictor of CH~4~ emission rates. An alternative explanation is that water depth serves as a proxy for water temperature at the sediment-water interface, with low temperatures in the hypolimnion of deep reservoirs constraining the response of methanogenesis, a temperature dependent process, to C loading [@yvon-durocher_2014].

Phytoplankton biomass can directly and indirectly influence the availability of C to methanogens. Algal derived C may sink to the sediments where it can be directly converted to CH~4~ via methanogens [@west_et_al_2015]. Phytoplankton can indirectly promote C delivery to sediments by releasing acidic polysaccharides into the water column which bind C particulates, both autochthonous and allochthonous, into flocs that settle into the sediment and stimulate methanogenesis [@martinez_2024]. Despite the well documented positive correlation between chlorophyll-*a*, a proxy for phytoplankton abundance, and CH~4~ emission rates [@west_2016; @deemer_et_al_2016; @delsontro_2018], the RF did not identify extraction-based or sonde-based chlorophyll-*a* measurements as important predictors. The SuRGE dataset was specifically designed to capture a broad range of chlorophyll-*a* concentrations (probabilistic site selection stratified by two productivity bins; @beaulieu_et_al_2026) and extraction-based chlorophyll-*a* concentrations across the 146 reservoirs ranged from `r dat_trans %>% {min(.$chla_lab_shallow, na.rm = TRUE)}` - `r dat_trans %>% {max(.$chla_lab_shallow, na.rm = TRUE)}` $\mu$g L^-1^. The lack of relationship between chlorophyll-*a* and CH~4~ emission rates may relate to temporal variability in chlorophyll-*a*, and potential lags between chlorophyll-*a* and CH~4~ emissions, which were not captured in this snapshot survey design. Chlorophyll-*a* can exhibit strong temporal variability at daily time-scales in response to patterns in wind and precipitation. Under calm conditions, phytoplankton may concentrate near the water surface where the SuRGE chlorophyll-*a* samples were collected; however, wind gusts may cause phytoplankton to mix throughout the epilimnion or advect to the shoreline, effectively diluting the chlorophyll-*a* concentration near the water surface. Phytoplankton can also undergo limited vertical migration to reach areas of the water column with physical and chemical conditions favorable to growth [@wetzel_2001]. The sonde-based measurements of chlorophyll-*a* made at each individual site using chlorophyll-*a* specific fluorescence probes may be further compromised by light sensitive photoquenching of the fluorescence yield of cyanobacteria and other algae. Daytime light exposure can suppress algal fluorescence by up to 79% relative to dark conditions [@rousso_2021], which may affect comparisons between SuRGE samples collected under different light conditions. The “snapshot-in-time” style of sampling used in the SuRGE project could not account for these patterns and may not reflect the availability of algal derived C in the sediments which integrates across the short-term temporal variation in phytoplankton abundance observed at the water surface.

#### Sulfate

Methane ebullition rates showed a negative, non-linear relationship with SO~4~^2-^ concentration, the fourth most important predictor in the local model **(Figures 2, 3)**. This finding joins similar reports from waterbodies in the North American Prairies region [@rimas_2026; @bansal_2023; @soued_2024]; in fact, the lowest rates of ebullition in the SuRGE dataset occurred in the Northern Plains ecoregion, a part of the broader North American Prairies region **(Figure 1)**. High SO~4~^2-^ may depress ebullition by favoring SO~4~^2-^ reducers over methanogens during their competition for labile C, and/or promoting CH~4~ oxidation coupled with SO~4~^2-^ reduction [@zhou_2024]. The partial dependence plot reveals that ebullition rates fall rapidly up to approximately 500 mg SO~4~^2-^ L^-1^, and beyond 1500 mg SO~4~^2-^ L^-1^ CH~4~ ebullition is negligible, suggesting that rising SO~4~^2-^ concentrations in freshwaters, driven by a range of human activities [@zak_2021], could ameliorate expected increases in future freshwater CH~4~ emissions [@bastviken_2025].

The diffusive CH~4~ model did not identify SO~4~^2-^ as an important predictor, which aligns with reports from the North American Prairies that ebullition rates are far more sensitive to SO~4~^2-^ than diffusive emission rates [@soued_2024], and that wetter, lower SO~4~^2-^ years promote hypolimnion CH~4~ accumulation without affecting diffusive emission rates [@rimas_2026]. This is likely because ebullition rates are directly linked to CH~4~ production and anaerobic oxidation in the sediments, which can be affected by SO~4~^2-^, whereas a number of other pathways (e.g., oxic CH~4~ production, water column CH~4~ oxidation) influence diffusive emission rates, thus obscuring the effect of sediment processes.

Taken together, the proportion of total CH~4~ emissions as ebullition (versus diffusion) declined with increasing SO~4~^2-^ concentration, with strong geographic patterning. Above approximately 100 mg SO~4~^2-^ L^-1^, ebullition accounted for \<50% of total CH~4~ emissions, and reservoirs with \>1000 mg SO~4~^2-^ L^-1^ had \<17% of total emissions as ebullition, aligning with a strong suppression of ebullition under high SO~4~^2-^ conditions. The reservoirs with the highest SO~4~^2-^ concentrations were located in the Northern and Southern Plains regions, likely related to underlying geology and potential agricultural runoff [@sun_etal_2026; @ligget_etal_2024] that have driven widely observed high SO~4~^2-^ concentrations in these eco-regions [@bansal_2023; @soued_2024; @sun_etal_2026].

#### Reservoir age

Reservoir age was not identified by the RF models as an important driver of CH~4~ emission rates. Previous work demonstrated that CH~4~ emission rates tend to decline as reservoirs age because terrestrial C that was inundated when the dam was built, a potential C source for methanogens, is progressively depleted. This pattern has been demonstrated with time-series investigations of individual reservoirs [@prairie_2021], metanalysis of published data from 89 globally distributed hydroelectric reservoirs [@barros_2011], and is integrated into a well-known model of reservoir GHG emission rates [@prairie_2021] that has been used to construct a timeline of global reservoir GHG emissions from 1900 - 2060 [@soued_2022]. While the SuRGE data includes reservoirs built between `r dat_trans %>% mutate(age = 2006 - year_completed) %>% {min(.$age)}` and `r dat_trans %>% mutate(age = 2006 - year_completed) %>% {max(.$age)}` years ago, relationships between age and CH~4~ emission rates were extremely weak (Pearson correlation coefficient = `r dat_trans %>% {cor(.$year_completed, .$ch4_ebullition, use = "pairwise.complete.obs")} %>% round(.,2)`, `r dat_trans %>% {cor(.$year_completed, .$ch4_diffusion, use = "pairwise.complete.obs")} %>% round(.,2)`, and `r dat_trans %>% {cor(.$year_completed, .$ch4_total, use = "pairwise.complete.obs")} %>% round(.,2)` for ebullition, diffusion, and total emission rates, respectively), and reservoir age was not identified as an important predictor in any of the RF models. It is unclear why this pattern isn’t evident in the SuRGE data, but it may be related to the relative importance of different C sources through time. While soil organic matter may fuel methanogenesis immediately after flooding, the progressive loss of this C could be offset by sediment loading from the watershed and the production of labile autochthonous C, particularly in systems with high watershed soil-erodibility and reservoir productivity. This explanation is supported by the partial dependence plot which shows total emission rates decreasing during the first 100 years followed by an increase in emission rates (**Figure S3**). Another explanation is that our sample population does not capture the youngest systems where CH~4~ emissions could be highest (after which time they exponentially decay). Still, the lack of an age effect is consistent with a recent study examining a 17-year dataset of CH~4~ concentrations spanning the initial reservoir creation on a large boreal reservoir, wherein no temporal trend was evident [@demarty_2026]. Projections of future emissions could be improved through a better understanding of the relative contributions of allochthonous and autochthonous C to reservoir CH~4~ production through time.

## Model Prediction Accuracy

### Local vs national models

Model performance metrics were marginally better for all local models, as compared to national models, when assessed at the log scale (i.e. the RF models predict log-scale emission rates). When the model predictions were back-transformed to linear space, differences in performance metrics between local and national models were smaller, and in some cases the national model outperformed the local model. Overall, these findings suggest that the accuracy of emission rate estimates derived from models that only require widely available data is similar to that of predictions from models which require on-the-ground measurements to quantify predictor variables. We anticipate that the accuracy of models based on nationally available datasets will only improve as new technology makes it possible to estimate aquatic physicochemical parameters with increasing accuracy and spatial resolution [@chen_etal_2022], and as datasets like this one inform process models to better represent key aspects of CH~4~ biogeochemistry with relatively limited input data [@maisonnier_2025]. One nuance in this comparison pertains to the accuracy of surface area estimates; we found one reservoir with a large discrepancy in the surface area estimated by the National Hydrography Dataset [@McKay_2012] vs. HydroLakes [@messager_2016]. This discrepancy was large enough to alter model performance depending on which value was selected. A limitation to the national models, however, is that they are not well-suited for predicting intra-reservoir patterns in CH~4~ emission rates. Spatially explicit estimates of CH~4~ emission rates within a reservoir will likely always require system-specific inputs. Inventory compilers should weigh the costs of generating the data required for local models against the accuracy gain when choosing the most appropriate modeling approach for their application.

### Comparison to other models

The local and national models developed here have slightly greater predictive accuracy than most other statistical models of reservoir CH~4~ emissions [@prairie_2021; @delsontro_beaulieu_2018; @deemer_2021]; although the process‐based Advanced Lake Biogeochemistry Model [@tan_2024] outperforms the statistical models (**Table 3**). Consistent with other modeling studies, model r^2^ was lower for ebullition than for the total or diffusion pathways. This finding is also consistent with the well documented episodic nature of ebullition in both time and space [@linkhorst_etal_2020]. One reason the r^2^ values reported here may exceed those of existing models is that our model was trained on a methodologically consistent dataset whereas many of the other existing models were trained using data harvested from the literature where measurement methodology likely varied across studies (but see @maisonnier_2025). Measurement methods provide varying degrees of spatial and temporal coverage and accuracy [@deemer_et_al_2016], thus combining measurements across studies may capture methodological noise that can not be explained by environmental drivers.

Another feature that distinguishes this work from previous studies is that SuRGE employed a probabilistic survey design to ensure an unbiased and representative sample of CONUS reservoirs. Site selection criteria vary across the literature, and it is likely that some reservoirs were selected for investigation due to special interest or convenience and therefore may not be a representative sample. This consideration extends to the selection of measurement sites within a reservoir. The SuRGE survey design ensured that a broad range of environmental conditions were captured within each reservoir (e.g. shallow and deep sites, inflow and open-water sites) whereas sampling intensity (e.g. number of sites) and site selection criteria are highly variable across literature studies. As a result, the SuRGE dataset reflects considerable intra-reservoir spatial variation in emission rates (mean intra-reservoir CH~4~ total coefficient of variation = `r dat_trans %>% mutate(across(c(lake_id, visit), as.numeric)) %>% group_by(lake_id, visit) %>% summarize(cv = (sd(ch4_total, na.rm = TRUE) / mean(ch4_total, na.rm = TRUE)) * 100) %>% ungroup %>% summarize(cv = mean(cv, na.rm = TRUE)) %>% pull(cv) %>% round(., 1)`%). While it is unclear how this spatial variation affected the predictive accuracy of the model, it provides a more realistic representation of the real-world variance in emission rates relative to the existing studies that were trained using data aggregated to a single value per reservoir regardless of how many sampling sites were included in the study.

Another advantage of modeling site-specific emission rates, as opposed to reservoir-scale values, is that the model can be used to make spatially explicit emission rate predictions within a reservoir. This difference could be important in reservoirs that exhibit strong spatial patterning in emission rate drivers, which is likely the norm rather than the exception. Reservoir zonation theory predicts that longitudinal patterns in width, flow, depth, and proximity to inflows lead to spatial patterns in productivity, sediment C, and temperature [@kimmel_1990]. We explore these patterns in William H. Harsha Lake in southwestern Ohio (lake_id 1031 in the SuRGE dataset) where previous surveys have documented spatial patterning in emission rate drivers (**Figure S5**). Our model predicts the greatest total CH~4~ emission rates (\~105 mg CH~4~ m^-2^ d^-1^) in shallow regions associated with tributary inflows and the lowest emission rates in the deep open-water areas (**Figure 5**), consistent with patterns documented in high-resolution surveys [@beaulieu_etal_2016]. While the model underpredicts the highest emission rates and overpredicts the lowest, relative to previously published data, when aggregated to the reservoir-scale, the predicted emission rate (89.05 mg CH~4~ m^-2^ d^-1^ (95% CI: 72.5 - 105.9)) agrees reasonably well with values observed during the SuRGE survey (`r emissions_lake_data %>% filter(lake_id == 1031) %>% select(ch4_total_lake) %>% pull %>% round(., 1)` mg CH~4~ m^-2^ d^-1^), particularly when viewed in context of the nearly `r (emissions_lake_data %>% slice_max(ch4_total_lake) %>% pull(ch4_total_lake) / emissions_lake_data %>% slice_min(ch4_total_lake) %>% pull(ch4_total_lake)) %>% round(., digits = -2)`-fold variation in reservoir-scale total emission rates across the dataset.

Most efforts to model reservoir CH~4~ emission rates with machine learning (ML) algorithms or frequentist statistical approaches apply a log transformation to the response variable. This improves ML performance [@death_fabricius_2000] and is often required to meet the assumptions of normality and homogeneity in frequentist statistical models. Model performance metrics, such as r^2^ between predicted and observed, are then routinely calculated and reported on the scale of the log transformed response variable. These performance metrics can greatly exceed those calculated after the model predictions have been back-transformed to the linear scale (**Table 2, Figure S2**), which is the scale CH~4~ inventory compilers use to estimate emissions. Model r^2^ values on the linear scale are \< 0.1 for diffusion and total emission rate but are a bit stronger for ebullition (0.16 - 0.32), demonstrating that the models explain little of the variation in emission rates at the linear scale. While r^2^ values provide a quantitative measure of model fit, sMAPE expresses prediction error relative to the known values and provides an intuitive measure of model error. sMAPE values for the local models are `r table2_object$table2_dat %>% filter(response == "ch4_diffusion", model_var_set == "local_vars_all") %>% pull(smape_linear) %>% round(., 1)`, `r table2_object$table2_dat %>% filter(response == "ch4_ebullition", model_var_set == "local_vars_all") %>% pull(smape_linear) %>% round(., 1)`, and `r table2_object$table2_dat %>% filter(response == "ch4_total", model_var_set == "local_vars_all") %>% pull(smape_linear) %>% round(., 1)`% for diffusion, ebullition, and total emission rates, respectively, which may be acceptable for some applications and not others. Inventory compilers should propagate linear-scale prediction uncertainty through their workflows to provide proper bounds on final inventory estimates.

### Model limitations

The SuRGE project was designed to emphasize inter and intra-reservoir spatial variation at the expense of temporal variation. Four lakes were sampled twice during the study with relative percent differences of `r emissions_lake_data %>% filter(lake_id %in% c(147, 148, 250, 281)) %>% select(lake_id, visit, ch4_total_lake) %>% pivot_wider(names_from = visit, values_from = ch4_total_lake, names_glue = "visit_{visit}") %>% mutate(perc_diff = abs(((visit_1 - visit_2) / visit_1) * 100)) %>% pull(perc_diff) %>% round(., digits = 0) %>% knitr::combine_words(.)`% in total emission rates across the site visits. Similar temporal variation has been observed at William H. Harsha Lake where reservoir-scale total CH~4~ emission rates of 198.5 (95% CI: 145 - 252) [@beaulieu_etal_2016], 235 (95% CI: 187 - 283) [@beaulieu_2014], and `r emissions_lake_data %>% filter(lake_id == 1031) %>% select(ch4_total_lake) %>% pull %>% round(., 0)` mg CH~4~ m^-2^ d^-1^ [@beaulieu_et_al_2026] have been reported based on "snapshot in time" sampling. A study at William H. Harsha Lake entailing continuous monitoring of ebullition at ten locations throughout the warm-weather season reported an average ebullitive emission rate of 823 mg CH~4~ m^-2^ d^-1^. The elevated emission rate observed during the continuous monitoring study is likely attributable to large, episodic bubbling events unlikely to be observed during \~24 hour funnel deployments [@varadharajan_2012]. This temporal variation limits the predictive accuracy of models trained on "snapshot in time" datasets.

# Conclusions

The performance and suitability of existing models for predicting reservoir CH~4~ emission rates are limited by the data used to train them. Although there has been a tremendous increase in the number of published studies over the last decade [@deemer_2021], differences in site selection criteria among studies makes it difficult to argue that literature data constitute a representative sample. Furthermore, differences in measurement approaches among studies have likely injected noise into the data that can't be explained by environmental drivers. Here we address those limitations by training models on data generated from a national-scale probabilistic survey that employed consistent methodology across all study sites. These models are suitable for predicting emission rates within and among any CONUS reservoir. The models perform as well, or better than, existing models, despite the training data containing nearly a `r (emissions_lake_data %>% slice_max(ch4_total_lake) %>% pull(ch4_total_lake) / emissions_lake_data %>% slice_min(ch4_total_lake) %>% pull(ch4_total_lake)) %>% round(., digits = -2)`-fold variation in reservoir-scale total CH~4~ emission rates.

Consistent with previous studies, the models identified reservoir morphology indices as important drivers of emission rates. The models also identified sediment C content as an important predictor. This latter finding mirrors reports that sediment CH~4~ production potential is partially controlled by sediment organic C content [@bodmer_2025] but to the best of our knowledge, this is the first study to document a relationship between sediment organic C and CH~4~ emissions at the national-scale. We also found that the effect of sediment C on emission rates is constrained by water depth, with deeper sites having a muted response to increased C availability relative to shallow sites. Such complex interactions are common in ecological data but have not been consistently tested for in reservoir CH~4~ studies.

Our models allow for reservoir CH~4~ emission rates to be predicted at multiple spatial scales and with varying degrees of data availability. Users with access to spatially explicit datasets of model predictors (e.g. site depth, sediment C, water temperature) can use the "local" model to make spatially explicit emission rate predictions within the reservoir(s) of interest (**Figure 5**). Users without access to detailed intra-reservoir data can use the "national" model to predict the mean emission rate at nearly any CONUS reservoir as the required predictor data (e.g. surface area, littoral fraction, remotely sensed DOC concentration) are available in national scale datasets, making this model iteration particularly useful for national-scale CH~4~ inventory exercises.

This effort was designed to address the limitations that literature data have imposed on existing models. While the models presented here represent an important advancement in this field of research, there is more work to be done. For example, the models are much less accurate at predicting high-end emissions, wherein back-transforming predictions to the linear scale explains less than 10% of the variation in total CH~4~ emission rates (**Table 2**). Prediction accuracy might be improved through the use of alternate modeling approaches. We chose RF modeling because this approach is known for high prediction accuracy and can accommodate important data features including hierarchical spatial structure (i.e. sites nested within lakes), interactions, and non-linear relationships. These features of the data can be accommodated by other modeling approaches including generalized additive mixed models (gamm) and Bayesian hierarchical models which may offer improved prediction accuracy. The SuRGE data could also be used to inform the development of statistical models [@prairie_2021] and process-based models [@delwiche_etal_2022; @tan_2024; @maisonnier_2025].
